story1289:
The valley was green and generous. The soil was dark and rich, and the people who farmed it were prosperous. They built stone houses with thatched roofs. They herded cattle that grew fat on the lush grass. They caught fish from the river that ran through the valley's center.

But prosperity bred contempt. The people forgot their obligations. They stopped making offerings to Were, the supreme god. They ate their harvests without giving thanks. They slaughtered their cattle without pouring blood at the crossroads. "We are self-sufficient," they said. "We need no god."

One old woman named Nyanjala was the exception. She still prayed at dawn. She still poured milk on the stones. She still whispered thanks before every meal. The other villagers mocked her. "Nyanjala is wasting her time," they said. "The gods are stories for children."

But Nyanjala was visited by a spirit in the night — a juogi, an ancestral messenger, who appeared as a figure made of mist and starlight. "Were is angry," the spirit said. "A great flood is coming. Take your family and your animals to the highest hill. Do not look back."

Nyanjala obeyed. She gathered her children, her grandchildren, and a few animals — a cow, some goats, a pair of chickens. They climbed to the top of the tallest hill in the valley and waited.

The waters came at dawn. They rose from the river, swelling and spreading, swallowing the fields, the houses, the roads. The people screamed and ran, but the water was faster. It filled the valley like a bowl being filled with water, rising higher and higher until only the hilltops remained above the surface.

Nyanjala watched from her hilltop as the valley became a lake. She watched her neighbors drown. She watched the world she had known disappear beneath brown water. She wept, but she did not look away.

When the waters finally settled, the valley was gone. In its place was a vast inland sea — what the world would later call Lake Victoria. Nyanjala and her family descended the hill and became the ancestors of the lakeside Luo.

To this day, the Luo fishermen who sail Lake Victoria make offerings before launching their boats — coins, tobacco, a splash of beer — to the nyawawa, the water spirits who guard the depths. The elders say the nyawawa are the descendants of those who drowned in the great flood, still trapped beneath the water, still angry at the god who punished them.

And Nyanjala — the old woman who listened when no one else would — is remembered as the mother of the lakeside people, the one who survived the flood because she never forgot to pray.
story1304:
Nzambi Mpungu was alone. Before the world, before time, before light, there was only the supreme creator and the dark waters that stretched to infinity. Nzambi Mpungu floated in the void, thinking thoughts that would become the universe.

When the moment of creation arrived, Nzambi Mpungu spoke. His voice was the first vibration — a sound so deep it split the waters. The waters above rose to become the sky. The waters below remained to become the sea. Between them, the earth appeared — wet, dark, and breathing.

Nzambi Mpungu shaped the sun and hung it in the sky to give light and warmth. He made the moon to govern the night and the stars to mark the seasons. He created plants — trees with broad leaves, grasses with thin blades, flowers with bright petals. He made animals — the leopard to prowl, the fish to swim, the bird to fly.

And then he made the first humans. He shaped them from clay, the same way Obatala shaped the Yoruba and Ngai shaped the Kikuyu. He breathed life into them and gave them laws: respect the earth, honor the spirits, share what you have, and do not kill without cause.

But humans are human. They quarreled. They lied. They stole. They killed. Nzambi Mpungu watched his creation descend into chaos and grew weary. "I have given them everything," he said. "They need nothing from me but obedience, and they cannot give even that."

Nzambi Mpungu withdrew. He climbed to the highest point of the sky and sat there, watching but no longer intervening. The world continued without him — or so the people thought.

But Nzambi Mpungu had not abandoned his creation. He left behind the Simbi spirits to guard the waters, the forests, and the mountains. He left the Nzambi — the earth goddess — to teach humanity arts, laws, and games. And he left the thunder, the rain, and the growth of crops as reminders that his power was still present, still active, still watching.

The Kongo say that Nzambi Mpungu is not distant. He is simply patient. He is waiting for humanity to grow up, to learn the lessons he tried to teach at the beginning. When that day comes, he will descend from the sky and walk among his people again.
story1305:
Nzazi was once a man. In the time before he became a spirit, he was a hunter of extraordinary skill — tall, strong, and proud. He could track a leopard through dense forest, outrun an antelope across open ground, and throw a spear with enough force to pierce stone.

But Nzazi grew too proud. He believed he was stronger than the spirits, wiser than the elders, more powerful than the gods. He climbed a great mountain, determined to reach the sky and challenge Nzambi Mpungu himself.

He climbed for days. The path grew steeper, the air thinner, the winds harsher. But Nzazi did not stop. He climbed until the trees disappeared, until the rocks gave way to ice, until the clouds were below his feet.

At the summit, he stood on the highest rock and shouted into the sky: "I am Nzazi! I am the greatest hunter! I challenge the creator!"

The sky answered. A bolt of lightning — thick, white, and blinding — struck Nzazi where he stood. The rock shattered. Nzazi's body was transformed. His bones became the framework of the sky. His eyes became the lightning that flashes during storms. His voice became the thunder that rolls across the plains.

Now Nzazi patrols the heavens during storms, hurling bolts of fire at those who break the sacred laws. When a tree is struck by lightning, the Kongo say Nzazi has visited judgment upon someone hiding beneath it. When a house is hit, Nzazi has punishing the wicked.

But Nzazi is not merely punitive. He is also a purifier. Lightning strikes burn away impurities — the spiritual contamination that accumulates when people live in discord. A lightning-struck field is considered blessed; the soil is purified and ready for new growth.

Those struck by lightning but left alive are considered chosen by Nzazi. They are marked — their skin bears strange patterns, their eyes hold a distant light. These survivors often become nganga, spiritual healers who can communicate with the sky spirits.

Lightning-struck wood is collected with reverence and carved into protective talismans. A piece of Nzazi's power, trapped in wood, can ward off evil spirits, heal the sick, and bring rain to drought-stricken fields.

The Kongo say: Nzazi is the proof that ambition, when it exceeds its proper bounds, becomes destruction. And that the same force that destroys can also purify — if you know how to listen to the thunder.
story1306:
Rabbit was tired of muddy puddles. Every other animal drank from the clear river — Elephant with his great trunk, Hippo with his wide mouth, even the small birds dipped their beaks in the flowing water. But Rabbit, who was the smallest and weakest, could only drink from puddles that stank of mud and mosquito larvae.

"I will fix this," Rabbit said to himself. He tied one end of a long vine to Elephant's trunk and the other end to Hippo's tail. Then he hid in the bushes and shouted:

"Pull!"

Elephant pulled east. Hippo pulled west. Each believed Rabbit was on the other end, and each was determined not to be outdone. They pulled and pulled, their feet gouging the earth, their breath coming in great gasps. The vine stretched. The ground shook.

Rabbit watched from the bushes, eating a stalk of grass. Hours passed. The sun climbed. Elephant's trunk ached. Hippo's tail throbbed. Neither would give up.

By evening, both had collapsed from exhaustion. The vine lay limp between them. Rabbit walked calmly to the river, knelt at the bank, and drank his fill.

"What happened?" Elephant asked, lifting his head.

"Rabbit tricked us," Hippo said, licking his sore tail.

But Rabbit was already gone, his belly full, his ears twitching with satisfaction.

Chief Leopard was furious when he heard the story. He was the king of the forest, and Rabbit's trickery was an insult to his authority. He set a trap — a pit hidden beneath leaves, baited with Rabbit's favorite food.

Rabbit found the pit. He studied it for a moment, then called out: "Leopard! I have caught something wonderful! Come see!"

Leopard ran to the pit and looked in — and fell in himself. Rabbit covered the pit with branches and walked away.

Leopard scratched and clawed his way out, but by the time he emerged, Rabbit was nowhere to be found. He had hidden in a thorn bush, where Leopard's great paws could not reach him.

The Kongo tell these stories to teach their children that intelligence and wit will always overcome brute force. Rabbit is small, but he is never defeated. Leopard is mighty, but he is never victorious. And in the animal kingdom, as in the human world, the clever survive while the strong merely endure.
story1307:
The Simbi live in the water. Not in the way fish live in water — passively, without thought. The Simbi live in the water the way a king lives in his palace: with authority, with awareness, with the power to grant or deny.

They are ancient beings who existed before humanity. When Nzambi Mpungu created the world, the Simbi were already there, swimming in the primordial waters, watching the creation unfold. They witnessed the first trees take root, the first animals take shape, the first humans draw breath.

The Simbi are guardians of esoteric knowledge. They know the properties of every plant, the names of every stone, the paths of every underground river. They know the future as well as the past, and they can reveal these secrets to those who ask properly.

"Properly" is the key word. The Simbi do not respond to casual requests. They do not answer to the curious or the greedy. They respond to those who respect the water — who keep the rivers clean, who do not overfish, who make offerings of food and prayer at the water's edge.

A person who honors the Simbi may receive visions — flashes of insight that reveal hidden truths. A person who disrespects the Simbi may be dragged into the depths, their body never recovered. A person who pollutes the water may go mad, their mind filled with the voices of angry spirits.

The nganga — the spiritual specialists of the Kongo — serve as intermediaries between humans and the Simbi. They conduct ceremonies at sacred river sites, offering food, cloth, and prayers. They interpret the Simbi's messages, which come in the form of ripples, bubbles, reflections, and dreams.

The Simbi remind the Kongo people that water is not merely a resource. It is a living, spiritual force that sustains all existence. To treat water as something to be used and discarded is to invite the wrath of beings far older and more powerful than any human.
story1308:
Mbidi Kiluwe came from the east, traveling through forests and across rivers until he reached the court of King Nkongolo Mwamba, the ruler of the Luba people.

Mbidi Kiluwe was unlike anyone the Luba had seen. His skin was lighter than theirs — not white, but the color of polished copper. His manners were refined. He ate in private, using utensils rather than his hands. He addressed people with formal titles and elaborate greetings. He spoke softly and never raised his voice.

King Nkongolo was Mbidi Kiluwe's opposite. He was crude, loud, and violent. He ate with his hands, spitting bones across the room. He ruled through fear, executing anyone who displeased him. His court was a place of chaos and terror.

Mbidi Kiluwe married Bulanda, Nkongolo's sister, and settled in the kingdom. He introduced new customs: the proper way to greet a superior, the proper way to eat, the proper way to speak in council. He taught the Luba that a king should govern through dignity, not violence.

But Nkongolo was jealous. He saw his people adopting Mbidi Kiluwe's manners and felt his own authority slipping. He plotted to kill his brother-in-law.

Mbidi Kiluwe learned of the plot and fled back to his homeland, leaving Bulanda behind. Before he left, he made a prophecy: "My son, who is not yet born, will return to this kingdom. He will be a king greater than Nkongolo. He will rule with wisdom and justice."

Bulanda gave birth to a son, Kalala Ilunga. The boy grew up hearing stories of his father's courtly ways and his uncle's tyranny. When he came of age, he returned to the Luba kingdom, challenged Nkongolo, and defeated him in combat.

Kalala Ilunga became the founder of the Luba Empire, establishing a dynasty that would rule Central Africa for centuries. The traditions of Luba kingship — bulopwe — were modeled on Mbidi Kiluwe's refined behavior: the emphasis on dignity, restraint, and wisdom over brute force.

The Luba say that Mbidi Kiluwe was more than a man. He was a culture hero — a figure who brought civilization to a people who needed it, who taught them that the mark of a great king is not the power to destroy but the grace to create.
